title: docmeta journey vocabulary (1.0.0-proposal.1)
description: The contract for a document that *defines* a critical user journey — the path a reader takes across several pages to get one thing done, and the other end of every `journeys: [cuj-install]` reference a page carries (docmeta:audience:1.0.0-proposal.1). This is the vocabulary that makes a docs set able to check its own strategy: a journey names its steps and, for each, the page that serves it, so the gaps are a query rather than a workshop. The document's name and summary stay `title`/`description` (docmeta:core:1.0.0-proposal.1), and the readers who take it are `personas`/`audiences` (docmeta:audience:1.0.0-proposal.1). Wired with an `overrides:` glob over the directory journeys live in; there is deliberately no `type: journey` constant, because `type` is the registry's most contested key — required and enumerated by diataxis:core:1.0, required by google:okf:0.1 — and pinning it would trade stackability for a claim the config already makes. "CUJ" stays the word people say; `journeys` is the key every page already uses to point here.

id.description: The stable anchor pages point at — `cuj-prove-value`. Required, where core leaves it optional: a journey that no page can claim membership in cannot be checked for coverage, which is the only reason to write one down.

trigger.description: What puts the reader on this path, in one line — `leadership wants proof the docs function delivers leverage`. Required, because a journey with no trigger is a table of contents: without the moment that starts it you cannot tell whether the first page is the right entry point, and you cannot tell two journeys over the same pages apart.

success-criteria.description: How you know the reader finished, in one line — `the champion can report merged doc PRs and time saved in a form leadership accepts`. Required, and the single most valuable field here: it is what turns a journey from a description into something testable, and what a reviewer checks the last step against. Stated as an outcome for the reader, never as a page they reached.

entry-point.description: Where the reader actually arrives — a route, a path, or a URL. Not derivable from `steps[0]`, and kept because it is often not the first step: readers land where search and marketing send them, then work backwards. The gap between this and the first step is itself a finding.

steps.description: The ordered path through the docs, one entry per thing the reader has to do. Order is the array's; there is deliberately no rank or weight field. Required and non-empty — a journey with no steps is a wish, and an empty list would read to a coverage report as a fully-covered journey, which is the failure this whole vocabulary exists to catch. Distinct from `next-steps` (docmeta:structure:1.0.0-proposal.1), which is one page's unordered follow-ons; these are one reader's ordered path. Deliberately **not** `uniqueItems`, unlike every one-or-list shape in this family: those are label sets, where a repeat is always noise, while this is an ordered record array — the same category as `command` and `success-exit-codes` in docmeta:evals:1.0.0-proposal.1, which are likewise not deduplicated. A journey that genuinely revisits a stage (review, then review again after a fix) is legal, and rejecting it to catch a copy-paste would trade a real shape for a cosmetic one.

evidence.description: What this journey was derived from — `customer-interviews`, `support-tickets`, `search-logs`. A journey nobody observed is a guess about how people read, and guesses drive real IA decisions. Recommendations, not a closed list.

evidence-strength.description: How far the evidence goes: `strong`, `moderate`, `thin`, `assumed`. Enumerated because a strategy-coverage report switches on it; absence means unassessed, not strong. Same ladder as the audience and persona vocabularies.

then.description: A step that hands off to another journey must name it: `coverage: cross-reference` with no `doc` says a different document owns this stretch without saying which, so a gap report cannot follow the edge and cannot tell the hand-off from an unassessed step. The same shape as the deprecation rule in docmeta:lifecycle:1.0.0-proposal.1 — a value that defers to something else must say what.

stage.description: What the reader is trying to do at this point, in their terms — `choose an access scope`, not `read the permissions page`. The only required key in a step, because a step that names only a document has recorded the answer without the question.

doc.description: The page that serves this stage — a route, a path, or a URL. When `coverage` says the page is missing, this is the route it *should* live at: writing the intended address down is what lets a gap turn into a ticket, and later into a redirect that still resolves.

coverage.description: How well the docs serve this stage: `covered` (a page does the job), `partial` (a page touches it but does not finish it), `missing` (no page — `doc` is the proposal), `cross-reference` (another journey owns this stretch, and `doc` names it). Enumerated because a gap report switches on it. This is deliberately **not** a boolean: `exists: true/false` cannot say *partial*, and a YAML boolean sharing a key with the strings `partial` and `ref` is a type trap — `no` and `off` are booleans in YAML 1.1, and TOML and JSON frontmatter type the same key differently again. Absence means unassessed, not covered; a report should count what is declared and say how much was not.

note.description: Why the coverage is what it is, for a human — `activity is visible; the reporting view is not documented`. The field that keeps a `partial` from being re-investigated every quarter.

step.description: One stage of the journey and the page that serves it. **Closed**, which is the one place this vocabulary catches typos — the same trade the `kg` envelope makes in docmeta:kg:1.0.0-proposal.1, and for the same reason: no generator competes for these keys, and a misspelled `coverage` on an open object is invisible, so a gap report reads the step as unassessed while the author believes it is filled in. That is a fail-open, and this record is the one the report is built on. A team that needs its own bookkeeping on a step — an issue link, an owner — prefixes the key `x-`, which is the documented escape hatch and stays greppable.

evidenceSource.description: One evidence source: a recommended value, or any non-empty string. The enum branch is advisory; the open branch keeps an org-specific research channel a correct document rather than a violation.

evidenceList.description: One evidence source, or a non-empty list of unique ones — the same one-or-list shape as stringList beside it and as kg's labelList, so a value ports between altitudes unchanged. The empty list is rejected on purpose: evidence: [] reads as evidence recorded, and it is the opposite of that.
